list.listitem: Suspect necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) in infants with significant clinical deterioration in conjunction with signs of abdominal distension, bilious emesis, and bloody stool. C
Initial evaluation should include CBC, blood gas, blood sugar, blood and CSF cultures, and AP and lateral abdominal radiographs. C
The diagnosis and staging of NEC is based on the Modified Bell's Staging Criteria (). C
Nonsurgical interventions include bowel decompression and rest, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and volume expansion for uncomplicated NEC. C
Indications for surgical intervention include pneumoperitoneum, portal venous gas, metabolic derangements, and poor splanchnic perfusion. C
The recommended surgical intervention is open laparotomy with drain placement. B
Measures to reduce the risk of NEC include human milk and probiotics. B

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is an inflammatory process affecting the bowel of infants, most often those born prematurely. The underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. Contributing factors are believed to include compromise of intestinal host defense and the infant's immune system, ischemia of the gastrointestinal tract, and mucosal breakdown secondary to bacterial overgrowth or exposure to enteral feedings.
The overall incidence of NEC is 0.3–2.4 cases per 1000 births, but increases to 4%–13% amongst very-low-birth-weight (VLBW) infants (birth weight <1500 g).
Greater than 90% of cases of NEC occur in premature infants, with a significant decrease in the incidence noted after 35 weeks’ gestational age and birthweight >1500 g.
Relative immaturity of the gastrointestinal tract and circulatory system and limitations in host defense are risk factors.

Risk factors associated with enteral feedings include the type of nutrition offered (human milk vs. formula), timing and more rapid rate of feeding advance, and increased osmolality of the initial feeding.

Other risk factors for the development of NEC include cyanotic congenital heart disease, polycythemia, exchange transfusion, umbilical catheters, asphyxia at the time of delivery, growth restriction in utero, cocaine exposure, and viral infections.
The exact pathophysiology is unknown.
Contributing factors include genetic predisposition, intestinal immaturity, microvascular injury/ischemia, highly immune-reactive intestinal mucosa, and abnormal microbial colonization.
Low-birth-weight infants who develop NEC have been found to have overrepresentation of gram-negative facultative bacteria in the gut microbiota.
Measures to reduce the risk of NEC include human milk and probiotics. B
Further research is needed regarding the role of lactoferrin and prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics. B
Infants provided human milk have a decreased incidence of NEC, and even of NEC requiring surgical intervention. However, fortification of human milk does not appear to increase the incidence of NEC.
A systematic review of human milk to prevent NEC in preterm infants found that it was effective, and that the benefit appeared to be greater in infants exclusively fed human milk.

A Cochrane review identified 60 RCTs with 11,156 comparing probiotics with placebo or no treatment in very or pre-term and low birthweight infants. In these infants, probiotics reduced the likelihood of NEC (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.65, NNT = 33). They may reduce mortality as well (RR 0.77, 95% CII 0.66 to 0.90, NNT = 50). There were too few data for extremely preterm and extremely low birthweight infants to draw firm conclusions.

A meta-analysis concluded that a probiotic mixture, Lactobacillus, and Bifidobacterium were optimal prophylactic probiotic choices in reducing the incidence of NEC (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.27–0.54 for probiotic mixture; OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37–0.91 for Lactobacillus, and OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50–0.94 for Bifidobacterium) in pre-term infants.

American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) guidelines gave a conditional recommendation to use a combination of probiotics with 2 or more species in preterm, low birth weight infants to prevent NEC.

Previous investigators had hypothesized that a decrease in nitric oxide levels may contribute to the development of NEC through intestinal ischemia. Arginine, a substrate for nitric oxide, may prevent NEC, but data are limited.
Neither oral nor intravenous immunoglobulins decrease the incidence of NEC.
Lactoferrin, which is a component of human milk, has a role in host defense and has been identified as a potential preventative agent in NEC.

Prophylactic enteral probiotics have been identified as a preventative intervention for NEC due to their ability to prevent mucosal bacterial translocation, enable elective exclusion of pathogens, and enhance host immune response.
However, prophylactic antibiotics may decrease the incidence of NEC, but are not widely recommended due to increased colonization of the gut with antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Differential.Differential_Features: Preterm infants, median postnatal age 7 days, presents with abdominal distension and bluish discoloration often without significant clinical decompensation; abdominal film shows pneumoperitoneum without pneumatosis, portal venous gas, or fixed dilated bowel loops
Clinical decompensation, abdominal radiographs may show ileus but no other findings of NEC

Differential.Differential_Name: Congenital bowel anomalies (Hirschsprung disease, bowel atresia, meconium ileus, volvulus, malrotation)
Misinterpretation of normal stool gas as pneumatosis intestinalis

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria include bilious gastric aspirate or emesis, abdominal distension, occult or gross blood in the stool; AND at least one of the following radiographic signs: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, pneumoperitoneum.
Modified Bell's Staging Criteria () are effective for staging NEC.
Suspect NEC in infants with significant clinical deterioration in conjunction with signs of abdominal distension, bilious emesis, and bloody stool.
Infants may have a history of increasing vital sign instability, apnea and bradycardia, feeding intolerance, bilious emesis, and bloody stool.

Abdominal examination can be notable for distension, absent bowel sounds, periumbilical erythema, abdominal wall discoloration, firmness to palpation, palpable abdominal mass, and abdominal tenderness/guarding.
Abdominal radiographs with pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, and/or pneumoperitoneum are highly specific for NEC.
Less specific findings seen on abdominal radiographs include dilated, thickened, or fixed bowel loops and paucity of bowel gas.
Blood cultures should be done to evaluate for concomitant bacteremia.
Obtain CBC, blood gas, and glucose to identify thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis and hyperglycemia, leukocytosis, and/or leukopenia.
Coagulation studies should be obtained if disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is suspected.
Numerous serum, urine, and stool biomarkers for NEC are being investigated, without proven clinical utility.
Decisions for interventions depend on stage and severity of NEC. C
Nonsurgical interventions of bowel decompression and rest, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and volume expansion are useful in cases of uncomplicated NEC. C
Indications for surgical intervention include pneumoperitoneum, portal venous gas, metabolic derangements, and poor splanchnic perfusion. C
Open laparotomy with drain placement is the recommended initial surgical intervention. B

Evaluation by a pediatric surgeon at the earliest detection of NEC (Bell's Stage 1B or higher) avoids delays in operative intervention. Uncomplicated NEC is managed by surgical and neonatal teams together in most centers.
The presence of gangrenous bowel, most evidently seen with perforated or necrotic intestine, remains the principal indication for surgical intervention.

The signs of deterioration consistent with necrotic bowel include peritonitis, worsening acidosis, persistent thrombocytopenia, rising leukocytosis or worsening leukopenia, hemodynamic instability, and hyponatremia. Presence of three or more of these signs is associated with complicated NEC.
Less clear indications include the following: fixed dilated loops of bowel on abdominal radiograph, gasless abdomen on abdominal radiograph, and persistent thrombocytopenia.

Surgical options include peritoneal drainage alone, laparotomy with diverting ostomy alone, and laparotomy with intestinal resection and primary anastomosis or stoma creation. Based on limited data from two small RCTs, a Cochrane review concluded that there was no apparent benefit or harm of peritoneal drainage over laparotomy. Since it is less invasive than laparotomy, it is generally the preferred initial surgical intervention. A systematic review found no evidence comparing enterostomy with primary anastomosis after resection.

Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy is recommended based on expert opinion to cover bowel flora. Between 20% and 45% of all cases of NEC are associated with sepsis. However, there is no evidence on the duration of antibiotics for NEC.
No single infectious etiology is known to cause NEC. There is also no evidence from randomized trials to support one antibiotic regimen over another.
A Cochrane review of four randomized trials with 227 neonates with NEC or sepsis concluded that pentoxifylline as an adjunct to antibiotic therapy reduced all-cause mortality.
A Cochrane review found no randomized trial evidence regarding the use of lactoferrin as an adjunct to antibiotics.
Endotracheal intubation may be preferred to ensure adequate ventilation and oxygenation, especially in the presence of apnea, circulatory collapse, or pulmonary edema.

NPO is recommended at first signs of NEC. A survey of pediatric surgeons found that most survey responders keep patients NPO for 5–10 days for medically treated NEC. The goal is to prevent emesis and abdominal distension in face of ileus. Volume expanders can be used to achieve modest changes in mean blood pressure. Blood products to correct anemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy and expand volume can be used.
Colonic strictures are a common postoperative complication from NEC, occurring in approximately 30% of cases.
Malabsorption may be the result of a number of factors related to surgical management, including gut dysmotility, bacterial overgrowth, and decreased bowel length.
Intestinal failure is managed with long-term parenteral nutrition. NEC has the highest rate of children weaning from parenteral support.
Postnatal growth failure is more common among infants with complicated NEC with a reduction in discharge weight Z-score of 0.24.
The mortality rate of NEC is as high as 35% but varies with severity of disease. Lower birth weight and hyperglycemia at presentation are associated with higher mortality.

A systematic review identified 38 observational studies with an overall mortality of 23.5% in all neonates with NEC. Overall mortality was 34.5% in neonates who underwent surgery, 40.5% in those who were extremely low birthweight, and 50.9% if both extremely low birthweight and requiring surgery.

NEC is independently associated with lower scores on developmental tests at 18 months corrected age. In a meta-analysis of 31 studies with 2403 infants with NEC, the incidence of neuro-developmental impairment was 40% (IQR 28%-64%). The incidence of neuro-developmental impairment was higher in infants with NEC who were treated surgically compared with those who were medically managed (43% vs 27%, p<0.00001, NNT = 6).
